name: Nora Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and run a heat-seam machine that tapes waterproof work jackets. My vocational certificate covered temperature settings and safe stops. I like a sleeve that survives the spray test; pulling melted tape off a jammed wheel is the sticky part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner repairs bicycles. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and about eleven months of expenses saved. My seam-line pay is higher than usual for an operator, and plenty of garment plants are nearby. I use AI every day to shorten fault notes into checklists, then test actual jackets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the workwear crew the AI pattern list is convenient, but a heavy jacket still needs its seams checked by hand. If the excitement fades, we can keep sewing good jackets. People buying workwear care whether the sleeve holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The seam-taping line pays me above the normal operator rate, and my partner's bicycle repair shop has regular customers. We have about eleven months of expenses saved, two school-age children and a mortgage. Plenty of garment plants are nearby. I like useful tools but don't need a revolution to stay employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep running the heat-seam machine and pull a jacket from each new roll to test its taped sleeve. I use AI daily to turn fault notes into a short checklist, then compare it with the actual garment. I will also show my nephew the safe seam check when he visits the workshop on Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The wages are coming in, and the children have a routine. A neat list is pleasant, but a dry sleeve is better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a real jacket contradict the log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Monday the log marked a jacket roll clean, but one seam lifted after we sprayed it. I stopped that roll and adjusted the heat wheel. A checklist cannot keep rain out of a jacket with a lifted seam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the repair shop affect the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop's regular repairs help with the mortgage, but my factory wage is the larger part of our budget. We set aside a reserve over several years. I would still check the school costs before buying another family bicycle.

say: An **AI checklist** cannot prove a work jacket is waterproof.
The line should **test taped sleeves** before releasing a new roll.
think: My **higher factory wage** and eleven-month reserve cover our mortgage now.
The **repair shop** and nearby garment plants provide further household options.
do: **Keep** heat-seaming jackets and spraying first sleeves each roll.
**Verify** AI fault checklists against actual garments before release.
feel: **Calm** about current wages and family routine.
S0.quote: A checklist cannot keep rain out of a jacket with a lifted seam.
fieldNote: Nora **uses AI daily** for fault summaries while relying on physical water tests.
Her **strong reserve** comes from years of wages; present factory pay remains the larger household income.

steps.text: Keep taping jacket seams and spraying first sleeves each roll

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI may handle workwear orders and shift lists before robots sew difficult seams. I would try a new camera check if the employer gives us paid time and a safe sample run. A sleeve that leaks should still stop the batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn another screen quickly, but a faster ordering system could combine two paid lines. Eleven months saved helps us wait for a real offer, yet losing my higher seam-taping wage would matter. My partner's bicycle repairs have busy and quiet weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the lead for the proposed paid roster and the last three leak rates. If the factory offers a paid guarded camera-control session with a trainer and sample jackets, I'll take it and learn the reject setting. I'll practise a new AI comparison of seam photos on anonymous test garments, checking every flagged sleeve with a spray test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possible merged line, though I like testing tools. I can compare a wet sleeve with a screen result before I trust either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test the camera?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would make a sample with a deliberately loose tape edge and see if the camera catches it. The trainer must show a safe stop before we use a live roll. I'd sign off only after both tests work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the rota matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare base shifts rather than peak-season overtime. If a line disappears, my partner and I would calculate the missing high-rate pay against school and mortgage bills. I want the written rota before changing childcare.

say: **AI ordering** may change workwear schedules before robots sew sleeves.
A **paid camera test** needs to catch a leaking seam.
think: A merged **seam-taping line** could cost my higher-paid hours.
Eleven months saved helps, but **shop repairs** cannot guarantee matching income.
do: **Check** proposed base shifts and recent leak rates.
**Learn** guarded camera controls if paid trainer-led sample place offered.
**Practise** new AI seam-photo comparison and verify flagged jackets with water.
feel: **Anxious** about potential paid-hour loss despite useful control tests.
S1.quote: A sleeve that leaks should still stop the batch.
fieldNote: Her **new AI learning** is seam-photo comparison, beyond her existing fault checklist.
Camera practice requires **offered paid safe time** with a trainer and sample jackets, while the roster remains unconfirmed.

steps.text: Compare proposed paid base shifts with leak rates before changing plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the workwear crew thinking AI could plan every jacket order by 2028, then capable robots around 2031 might tape and test seams. I would ask for an honest paid-role list before arguing about a machine we have not seen. Families need dates, not rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when robots can do the hands-on work. My higher taping wage could disappear, and the repair shop alone may not cover the mortgage. Eleven months saved and plenty of nearby garment plants give us time to look, but their wages might be lower. I cannot assume our children cost less when a robot arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the factory for a written staffing date and paid quality openings. If it offers funded paid-time training in guarded waterproof testing with a real place, I'll enrol. If my hours fall, I'll apply to posted safe local garment jobs only if base pay and school hours fit; after qualifying, I'll also apply for posted local waterproof-testing jobs under the same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the higher wage, but able to compare real openings. I would not leave a full paid shift for a training flyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should waterproof training teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test should make me seal a jacket sleeve, soak it and measure where water gets through. I'd practise with a trainer on a stopped line. A dry-looking seam can still soak a child's arm on the way to school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which garment job would you take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A garment vacancy needs a posted base rate and shift time, not a promise of peak-season hours. I'd compare the rate against the mortgage and the shop's slower months. If it falls short, I keep looking.

say: **2028 thinking AI** changes jacket orders before robots sew around 2031.
Families need a **written staffing date** and real paid quality openings.
think: At **48**, I might lose the higher seam-taping wage.
Eleven months saved and **many garment plants** permit a search without equal-pay certainty.
do: **Ask** factory for written robot staffing and paid quality posts.
**Enrol** in funded paid guarded waterproof testing if offered.
**Apply** to posted safe local garment or qualified testing if hours fall and pay fits.
feel: **Anxious** about higher-wage loss with reserve and local options.
S2.quote: A dry-looking seam can still soak a child's arm on the way to school.
fieldNote: She faces possible **higher-wage loss** but has eleven months saved and many local garment employers.
The **garment fallback** and qualified testing applications require posted safe local work, sufficient base pay and workable school hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI may plan jacket orders in 2031 and capable robots might sew around 2034. Five years gives us time to learn another task on a real machine. I would rather see offered paid seats than a folder of course names.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 51 when robots do the physical seam work. My wage may still pay most of the mortgage, and the children will be older but not necessarily independent. The reserve lets us choose carefully; I would still need a posted job after any training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the seam-taping job and put new money from each full higher-rate pay month into our reserve after bills. I'll ask for a recognized machine-maintenance certificate with covered fees, paid release and guarded practice. If offered, I'll enrol; once qualified, if taping hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local maintenance only when base pay and travel fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a later crew change, with time to check the terms. I can learn while the line still pays me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must hands-on maintenance cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trainer should have me isolate the heat wheel, fit fresh tape and test a rejected sleeve before restarting. I would need that on paid time. I don't want a seam-machine maintenance certificate from watching someone else's hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the maintenance post is actually local and how often it requires travel to other plants. A higher hourly rate can vanish into unpaid travel. The regular wage must cover our bills.

A **paid practical place** matters more than course names.
think: At **51**, I may still need my taping wage for the mortgage.
Our **strong reserve** helps choose but does not create a posted role.
do: **Save** new money from full higher-rate pay after bills.
**Enrol** in maintenance if fees, paid release and guarded practice covered.
**Apply** for posted safe local maintenance if qualified, hours fall, pay and travel fit.
feel: **Uneasy** about later crew changes with present wages intact.
S3.quote: I don't want a seam-machine maintenance certificate from watching someone else's hands.
fieldNote: Her **new reserve deposits** come from future full higher-rate wages after bills.
The **maintenance application** follows offered qualification and reduced hours, with posted safe local pay and workable travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI may plan workwear orders by 2036 and capable robots could tape seams around 2039. A decade lets parents teach practical skills while the factory still pays. I would ask for real training seats before telling anyone to change jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when physical robots arrive. The children may be grown, but I cannot assume the mortgage or shop costs have vanished. Eleven months saved gives a bridge and many garment plants give choices if they still hire at a useful rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the seam line and pay extra mortgage principal from new full-wage money after household bills. I'll ask my aunt, who repairs sewing machines, whether her workshop posts paid apprenticeships with guarded practical time. If a funded paid place is offered with a trainer, I'll take it; after qualifying, if seam hours fall, I'll apply for posted safe local repair work only if regular pay and travel suit us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a distant change, though present wages are sound. I can wait for a written offer and still learn from family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What can your aunt actually tell you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt can explain which parts break on an industrial sewing machine and what a real apprentice earns. My aunt who repairs sewing machines cannot promise me a paid apprentice seat. I'd ask the workshop for the paid timetable and guard rules in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a repair job viable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the repair posting's base rate and travel days with our mortgage and the children's routine. A job with irregular unpaid travel would not suit us. I could keep earning at the factory while looking.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could cut the higher-paid seam line before a different job is ready. A written staffing date, an offered funded paid practical place and posted safe local work with enough base pay would help. I would check our family schedule too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tests the first jacket after a robot seals its sleeves. Rain will find a lifted seam even if the machine's report says every jacket passed.

headlineQuote: Rain will find a lifted seam even if the machine's report says every jacket passed.
portrait: **Nora**, 43, runs a waterproof-jacket seam machine with a vocational certificate and daily AI use for fault notes.
She and her bicycle-repair partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage, with eleven months saved and high operator pay.
Her **traditional outlook** values family craft advice and paid apprenticeships, while she learns useful technology early.
Fast robots make her **anxious** about the high wage; real course places and posted garment work shape her plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable seam-taping robots around 2031 and cut her higher-paid line.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing date**, offered funded paid practical training and posted safe local pay would help.
